newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OECD sees New Zealand growth slowdown.
newsitem.headline: OECD sees New Zealand growth slowdown.

text.p: Monetary policy in New Zealand is likely to remain tight, restraining economic growth, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development said in a semi-annual report.
The report -- prepared before the country's new centre-right coalition government was formed -- warned that there appeared to be significant downside risks to the country's growth outlook.

High interest rates and a continued appreciation of the exchange rate had led to a slowdown in growth, with much of the adjustment coming from the net foreign balance and investment, it said. It forecast that growth in real gross domestic product (GDP) would slow to 2.3 percent in 1996 from 3.6 in 1995, then pick up to 2.9 percent in both 1997 and 1998.

The report was prepared before the nationalist New Zealand First Party announced on December 10 that it had formed a coalition with the conservative National Party, in power since 1990. The market's initial response was a dip in short-term interest rates and the New Zealand dollar.
The OECD said recent and planned future tax cuts should generate a consumption-led recovery. The new government has since delayed by one year tax cuts that were to come into effect in mid-1997.

"Nevertheless, with underlying inflation above the upper limit of the target range and as yet only limited signs of an easing of pressures on the housing and labour markets, monetary conditions are likely to remain firm," the OECD said.
It said the Reserve Bank would want to see clear signs that inflation would return to its target range, which might not be the case before mid-1997.
The new coalition government has subsequently widened the target range, to 0-3 percent from 0-2 percent.
Slower growth should relieve capacity constraints and ease upward pressure on inflation, the report said.
Unemployment was forecast barely changed at 6.2 percent in 1996, with the rate unlikely to fall significantly below six percent, over the next two years, the report said.
